answers.answer: The API producer publishes the export job ID and inputs. Broker confirmation of the handoff permits a truthful accepted response with that ID, not a ready file. The broker holds the job until a worker receives it; the worker renders and saves the required file and ready status, then acknowledges processing. Users see pending while waiting, ready once the required result is saved, and failed on terminal failure. Because these users can continue with a job ID, the two-minute render can happen after the five-second request ends. Login remains synchronous because access requires the final authorization result first. Operating the broker and workers and tracking status are added costs.

evidence.quote: Publishes a message containing the job ID and inputs. An API must confirm the handoff before telling the client the job was accepted.
Receives the message, saves the required result and ready status, then acknowledges processing to the broker. A consumer acknowledgement lets the broker retire that delivery.
Acceptance confirms responsibility for the job, not completion. Return a job ID and make pending, ready and failed status observable; ready means the required result has actually been saved.

Keep decisions synchronous when the next action requires their result. Authorization must finish before granting access to a private resource; queueing that decision cannot justify granting access immediately.
The trade-off includes operating the broker and workers, tracking status, handling duplicates and retries, and watching backlog. A queue does not solve sustained overload.

answers.answer: With at-least-once delivery the broker may deliver the job again after the unacknowledged committed credit. Acknowledging first risks retiring the delivery before a crash prevents the credit, losing the work. Reuse one stable business-operation ID across attempts. Insert it into a durable processed-jobs table with a unique constraint and apply the credit in one database transaction: both commit or neither does. A duplicate ID skips the effect. A separate check then write can race or crash between steps. This protects the database credit from repetition; it does not establish universal exactly-once delivery or make external effects atomic.

evidence.quote: A worker commits its database changes, then crashes before acknowledging. With at-least-once delivery, the broker can deliver the job again. Acknowledging first instead risks losing the work if the worker crashes before saving it.
Repeating the same operation has the same effect as doing it once. Reuse a stable business-operation ID across retries, not a new ID per attempt.

In one database transaction, insert that ID into a durable processed-jobs table with a unique constraint and apply the job's database effect. Commit both or neither. A duplicate ID skips the effect. A separate check followed by a write can race or crash between steps.
That transaction protects its database effects. It does not make an external email or payment atomic, or turn delivery into a universal exactly-once guarantee.

answers.answer: Retry the temporary image-store outage with increasing delays and a finite attempt or time budget, since recovery is plausible and immediate retries can deepen the outage. On budget exhaustion, isolate the job in a dead-letter queue and expose failed status. Isolate the unsupported-format message because waiting cannot repair it. Isolation lets healthy jobs continue. Before replay, fix the cause and check whether an earlier attempt already applied an effect; replay still requires duplicate safety. The lesson gives no numeric delay or budget, so those values remain unspecified.

evidence.quote: A temporary storage outage may recover. Retry with increasing delays and a finite attempt or time budget; immediate retries can deepen the outage.
An unsupported input format will not improve with waiting. Isolate it, or any job that exhausts its budget, in a dead-letter queue for investigation and expose failed status.
Healthy jobs can continue. Before deliberately replaying a failed job, fix its cause and check whether an earlier attempt already applied an effect. Replay still needs duplicate safety.

answers.answer: The final quantity may incorrectly be 5: set-to-2 finishes first and the older set-to-5 overwrites it. Delivery order does not determine completion order. Serialize effects per item ID, holding later events while earlier ones run or retry; different items can proceed concurrently. If an earlier job is isolated, repair or cancel it before releasing dependent updates. One busy item becomes a throughput bottleneck because its dependent work must wait.

evidence.quote: Delivery order and completion order are different. Two updates set the same address to old, then new. Workers receive them in order, but the slower old update finishes last and overwrites new.
Serialize effects per entity ID: keep later updates waiting while an earlier one runs or retries. Different entities can still run in parallel. A busy entity becomes a throughput bottleneck.
Moving the earlier job to a dead-letter queue does not resolve the dependency. Decide how to repair or cancel it before releasing dependent updates.

answers.answer: Backlog grows by approximately 120 - 80 = 40 jobs per second. Increasing oldest-job age shows growing waiting time and the risk of violating the promised delay. Bound worker concurrency to the image store safe limit. Apply producer backpressure by throttling, visibly rejecting new requests as busy, or explicitly deferring only within an agreed limit. Buffering is finite: capacity must later catch up before storage, retention, or allowed-delay limits. More workers help when workers are the bottleneck and downstream services have spare capacity. Here the image store is already at its safe concurrency limit, so adding worker concurrency cannot be assumed to help.

evidence.quote: If 100 jobs arrive each second and 70 finish, unfinished work grows by 30 jobs per second. Watch backlog and oldest-job age: a growing wait can violate the promise to the client.
Storage and retention are finite. A queue can absorb a burst only if capacity later catches up before those limits or the allowed delay are reached.
Bound worker concurrency to protect the database. Throttle or reject new requests with a visible busy response, or explicitly defer them within an agreed limit.
More workers help when workers are the bottleneck and downstream services have spare capacity. If the database is already saturated, more workers increase contention instead.

answers.answer: A work queue distributes purchases among competing workers, so it does not independently give every event to billing and analytics; failed deliveries may repeat. A retained log allows billing and analytics groups to each independently read every purchase. Each group tracks its own offset for each partition, and workers within a group share partitions. Committing progress does not delete retained records. Analytics can rewind and replay the last day only if all required events still remain under retention. Ordering is per partition, not global, so adding partitions or consumers does not create universal global order. History and offsets also do not themselves guarantee exactly-once external effects; recording progress is not proof that an arbitrary business effect succeeded or was atomic.

evidence.quote: A work queue divides jobs among competing workers; it does not give every independent application every job. Failed deliveries can still repeat.
A retained log keeps event history for consumers to read independently. If billing and analytics each need every purchase event, separate consumer groups can track their own progress.

In Kafka, a partition is an ordered slice of the log. Each group tracks its own position, called an offset, for each partition. Workers within a group share the partitions. Committing an offset records progress; it does not delete the event.

A group can rewind and replay only while the required events remain under the retention policy. Ordering is per partition, not global. Retained history and offsets do not by themselves make external effects exactly once.
These acknowledgements cover different boundaries. Neither makes a broker operation atomic with a database write or proves an arbitrary business effect succeeded.
